claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — six resolved (three confirmed, two refuted, one expired), two open, three new

Every open conditional claim (§4B — a specific, falsifiable test this system logs before the outcome is known, then grades against the data) is checked against the latest closes before any new narrative is written. The 10-13 and 10-14 runs failed closed, so three claims due on those days are graded today on their original five-session windows. Prices are Yahoo closes recorded in data/raw/claims_check_2026-10-15.json.

  • CL-0039 refuted — Oracle’s 10-08 drop as the start of a durable repricing of AI-financing risk. The refute line was a close of $142.47 (+5% from the $135.69 base) within five sessions. Oracle closed at $143.20 on Tuesday 10-13, +5.53%. Refuted, plainly. Then on Wednesday it fell 8.83% to $130.55, 3.79% below the base. The test asked about a snapback, and the snapback happened; it just didn’t last. Wednesday’s reported reasons are in Movers, below.
  • CL-0040 refuted — T-Mobile’s 10-09 drop on SpaceX’s spectrum deal as a durable repricing. The refute line was a close of $156.01 (+5%). T-Mobile closed at $157.79 on Wednesday, +6.20% from the $148.58 base, three sessions in. AT&T ($23.05, +3.92%) and Verizon ($44.42, +6.65%) also rebounded from their 10-09 closes. Raymond James upgraded T-Mobile on Oct 12 (to Outperform; TipRanks reported it as Buy), calling SpaceX competition fears “overblown, as they are 3+ years away” (Investing.com, Seeking Alpha, TipRanks). CNBC argued on Oct 13 that the SpaceX threat to telecom is real. No T-Mobile-specific news turned up for Wednesday.
  • CL-0037 confirmed — Caterpillar’s 10-07 downgrade selloff as a durable repricing. Caterpillar never got near its $854.52 refute line (+5%). It closed the window at $748.98 on Wednesday, 7.97% below the $813.83 base, after falling 3.33% Tuesday and 3.08% Wednesday. Bloomberg on Wednesday framed Caterpillar’s slide as oil prices, bond yields and doubts about the AI trade weighing on industrials. No single company catalyst was reported for Tuesday.
  • CL-0035 confirmed (due 10-14) — the second storage selloff as a genuine re-rating, not another whipsaw. At the window’s end (Tuesday 10-13), Seagate was at $747.20 (−7.25% from $805.63) and Western Digital at $380.71 (−7.38% from $411.04). Neither came near a +5% snapback. Both fell further Wednesday, outside the window. StockStory tied Tuesday’s storage drop to China’s CXMT announcing denser server-memory plans, which prompted a reassessment of tight memory supply. CXMT makes memory chips, not hard drives, so this system reads the link as sentiment across storage names rather than a direct competitive hit.
  • CL-0032 confirmed, narrowly (due 10-13) — C.H. Robinson’s RXO-deal selloff as durable skepticism. The best close in the window was $142.31 (+1.21% from the $140.61 base), far from the +5% refute line ($147.64). The window ended at $139.75 on Monday 10-12, 0.61% below the base. “Flat-to-lower” held, though only just. No new named-outlet news on the RXO deal turned up since its Oct 5 announcement.
  • CL-0033 expired, unresolved (due 10-13) — Lennar’s Q3-miss selloff as rate-linked deterioration. Confirmation needed the 10-year to stay at or above 5.31%, and it never did after the base day (5.22% to 5.28%). The refute side needed a +5% snapback ($78.16); Lennar’s best close was $77.60 (+4.25%). It ended the window at $74.65, +0.28%. Neither side was met, and no credible named-outlet reason for the window’s moves surfaced.
  • CL-0038 open, one session left — Coherent’s 10-08 optics selloff as a genuine re-rating. Coherent fell 9.19% Wednesday to $263.32, 12.91% below the $302.35 base. Only a close at $317.47 or higher today (+20.6% in one session) refutes it. Graded tomorrow.
  • CL-0041 open, confirmation now out of reach — Thursday 10-08’s junk-spread widening as the start of credit repricing. Confirmation needed every print dated 10-09 to 10-15 to stay at or above 3.15%. The print dated 10-09 came in at 3.11%, so that path is closed. Prints since: 3.11% (dated 10-12) and 3.16% (dated 10-13). Only a print at or below 3.03% refutes it; otherwise it expires. Graded on the 2026-10-19 run.
  • CL-0042 opens — Wednesday’s AI-hardware selloff (SMH −3.97%; Dell, Ciena, Lumentum, Coherent, Oracle and Marvell down 8.7% to 11.3%) is the start of a durable repricing of the AI-infrastructure trade, not a one-day rotation. Test: SMH closes at or below $564.74 on Wednesday 10-21 (confirms); any close at or above $588.12, Tuesday’s close, from today through 10-21 refutes it; anything else expires. Graded on the 2026-10-22 run.
  • CL-0043 opens — if Wednesday was a risk event rather than a rotation, credit says so on the day (Unit 3’s tie-breaker). Test: the HY OAS print dated 10-14 comes in at 3.21% or wider, 5bp or more above the 3.16% dated 10-13 (confirms); at or below 3.16% refutes it; 3.17%–3.20% expires. Graded tomorrow.
  • CL-0044 opens (event day, §4E) — today’s 8:30am data move the 2-year in the direction of the surprise. If PPI (consensus +0.5% m/m in this system’s calendar) and retail sales (+0.3%) both print above consensus, a 2-year close at 4.85% or higher confirms and 4.82% or lower refutes. If both print below, 4.79% or lower confirms and 4.82% or higher refutes. Mixed or in-line prints expire. Graded tomorrow. Logged up front: CNBC reported Treasury yields falling overnight, before the data.
dashboard_interp_html:
On CPI day, short rates rose and long rates fell. The 2-year rose 3bp to 4.82% (z +1.97) and the 3-month bill 2bp to 4.28% (z +2.36, tied with Sep 28 for its highest reading of the past six months). The 10-year fell 2bp to 5.19% (z +1.99) and the 30-year 4bp to 5.52% (z +1.78). Every maturity is still flagged: well above its six-month average. Because the short end rose while the long end fell, the curve flattened. The 2s10s spread (the 10-year minus the 2-year) narrowed 5bp to 37bp, and 11bp over the past week. The front end tracks what the market expects from the Fed, so the rise there is a firmer Fed path being priced (Unit 1). For scale, the 10-year sits at the 86th percentile of the last 30 years but only the 48th since 1962. The 30-year reads the same way: 84th over 30 years, 48th since 1977.

Tuesday’s real-yield data filled in. The 10-year real yield (what a Treasury pays after inflation, dated 10-13) eased 3bp to 2.88%, and the 10-year breakeven (the bond market’s inflation forecast) held at 2.33%. So Tuesday’s small 10-year dip was all real rates (Unit 2). The CPI-day split arrives tomorrow.

Junk spreads widened again into the selloff. HY OAS (the extra yield investors demand to lend to junk-rated companies, dated 10-13) rose 5bp to 3.16% (z +3.18, the day’s largest flag). That’s wider than on all but one day in the past six months: Oct 1’s 3.24%. It sits at the 65th percentile of its own ~3-year record here, so it’s unusual lately, mid-range on its short full record. IG OAS (the investment-grade version, dated 10-13) held at 0.83% (z +1.60, flagged because it has crept up from its six-month average, not because it moved). The credit print for Wednesday itself, the selloff day, arrives tomorrow. It is the tie-breaker CL-0043 tests (Claims, above).

The dollar (DXY, z +2.19) rose 0.36% to 102.55, just under Monday’s 102.58. That’s the 72nd percentile since 1971 and the 82nd over 30 years. SOFR (the overnight bank funding rate, dated 10-13) rose 2bp to 3.89% (z +2.43). ON RRP (money funds’ overnight parking spot at the Fed) was $0.20 billion (z −0.54, calm). The Fed’s balance sheet and the Treasury’s cash account (TGA) carry the 10-07 weekly readings until this afternoon’s release.

The index fell 1.1%; the average stock fell half that. The S&P 500 fell 1.11% to 7,718.94, 1.28% below its Oct 6 record close. The Nasdaq fell 1.88%. The equal-weight proxy (RSP, the average S&P stock) fell 0.57%, against 1.08% for the cap-weighted SPY. So the biggest companies did most of the falling. Since Oct 7, RSP is up 0.71% while SPY is down 0.98%. The chip fund SMH fell 3.97% and is down 10.71% since the Oct 6 record day. Small caps are the exception to the “average stock held up” story: the Russell 2000 fell 1.93% to 2,729.53 (z −2.12), its lowest close in six months and 11.04% under its Aug 14 high.

Why this matters: short-term rates rising again keeps CD and money-market yields high for savers, and a firmer Fed path is the backdrop for every rate-sensitive purchase, from car loans to mortgages (30-year mortgage rate 7.40% in the latest weekly survey). For portfolios, the split matters more than the index: a client who owns an S&P 500 fund felt a 1.1% day, while a client in health care or staples funds may have had a gain.
chart_of_day_why: Mechanical rule (§6.5a, largest |z| flag) points to HY OAS: z +3.18, dated 10-13, ahead of SOFR’s +2.43 and the 3-month bill’s +2.36. It is also the series that decides today’s story. Credit is the tie-breaker between a rotation and a risk event (Unit 3), and the print dated 10-14, the selloff day, arrives tomorrow (CL-0043). The chart marks Oct 1’s 3.24% peak and Oct 8’s 3.15% (CL-0041’s base). For §4F scale: 3.16% sits at the 65th percentile of the high-yield spread’s ~3-year record here, so it’s unusual against the past six months but mid-range on its short full record.
history_html:
The level, and the run. The 10-year closed at 5.19%, below this run’s 5.31% peak of Oct 5. Before this run, it was last this high only briefly, in July 2007. Against the last 30 years that’s high (86th percentile); since 1962 it’s average (48th).

July 2007, then vs. now. Long-term rates match closely: the same 10-year (5.19%), similar real yields, breakevens and term premium (a Fed model’s estimate of the extra yield for lending long). The short end does not. The Fed’s rate was 5.22% then; SOFR is 3.89% now. So the 3-month-to-10-year spread is +91bp today against +24bp then. In 2007, high short rates did the squeezing. Today the long end carries the weight, and mortgages cost more (7.40% now, 6.63% then).

Speed is the unusual part. The 10-year is up 101bp this year, the 9th-largest rise through this date in 64 years. A 12-month rise this big has started 12 times since 1963. From each start, stocks were lower a year later in 5 of 12, against 24.4% for any 12-month stretch. A recession began within two years in 5 of 12 (4 different recessions), against 27.4% normally. Twelve is a small sample.

Wednesday’s drop, sized. A 1.11% S&P 500 decline comes about 30 days a year; this was the 17th this year. For the index, an ordinary bad day. The damage was concentrated (Movers, below).

Why this matters (client-ready): “Long-term rates are back where they were in mid-2007, but the Fed’s own rate is well below 2007’s, so this is the bond market charging more to lend for ten years, not the Fed squeezing. When rates rose this fast before, stocks were lower a year later in 5 of 12 cases, versus about one in four normally: a small sample, not a forecast.”
concept_unit: Unit 6 — Positioning & sentiment vs. fundamentals, segment 1
concept_title: Breadth: the index versus the average stock
concept_html: Units 1 through 5 were about the plumbing: rates, inflation, credit, liquidity and the dollar. Unit 6 turns to the stock market itself, and to one question: is a move about what companies are worth, or about how crowded a trade had become? Its first tool is breadth (how many stocks join a move). The S&P 500 is cap-weighted: the biggest companies count the most, so a handful of giants can drag it. An equal-weight version gives every company the same vote, so it tracks the average stock. Wednesday shows the gap. SPY (cap-weighted) fell 1.08%; RSP (equal-weight) fell 0.57%. Since Oct 7, RSP is up 0.71% while SPY is down 0.98%. When the index falls harder than the average stock, the selling is concentrated in the biggest, most popular names. That pattern fits a crowded trade being unwound better than a broad growth scare, which would hit most companies at once. It’s a reading, not a proof: breadth says where the selling was, not why. Small caps complicate it. The Russell 2000 fell 1.93% to its lowest close in six months, so smaller companies were not spared. And credit, the tie-breaker from Unit 3, hasn’t reported on Wednesday yet (CL-0043).
client_translation: When the headline index drops but the average stock barely moves, it’s usually a few big, popular names coming down, not the whole market, so look at what you actually own before reacting to the headline.
masthead_title: AI stocks led the S&P 500’s biggest drop since July after a hot inflation report, while health care and staples rose.
regime_line: After a hotter-than-expected inflation report, short-term Treasury yields and the dollar rose and the odds of another Fed hike jumped (tightening), and an AI-stock rout gave the S&P 500 its biggest drop since Jul 29 (−1.11%). The selling was narrow: chips fell 3.97%, health care and staples rose more than 2%, and the average stock fell about half as much as the index.
story_html:
The press has one story this morning: inflation plus AI. The Associated Press headlined Wednesday’s close “US stocks drop to their worst day since July as inflation worsens,” the S&P 500’s “fifth loss in the six days since setting its all-time high.” Reuters led with “Nasdaq ends sharply lower as hot inflation data stirs rate-hike worries,” Bloomberg with “Stocks Fall on Inflation Woes as Chip Rout Deepens,” and CNBC with “S&P 500 drops 1%, dragged down by hot inflation data and sell-off in AI-related stocks.” The trigger was September’s consumer price index (CPI): +3.7% from a year earlier against 3.6% expected. Core prices (excluding food and energy) rose 0.3% on the month and 2.6% on the year, each a tenth above forecasts (CNBC, citing the Dow Jones consensus). Gasoline rose 9.1%, more than half of the monthly gain (CNBC). On AI, much of the framing is about money: CNBC said worries came to the fore about tech companies outside the “Magnificent Seven” taking on too much debt to fund the AI boom, and CNN said higher yields and sticky inflation make the data-center buildout more expensive to finance. This morning Reuters leads with “Nasdaq futures dive 1% as AI rout deepens on debt concerns,” and South Korea’s Kospi fell about 7.6% on Thursday, with a 20-minute trading halt (Korea Herald, Aju Press). The Wall Street Journal’s and Financial Times’ own pages couldn’t be reached from this system’s search this morning, so their framing isn’t reported.

Does the data confirm it? On inflation and the Fed, yes, at the short end. The 2-year rose 3bp, the 3-month bill 2bp and the dollar 0.36%. CME FedWatch put the odds of an October rate hike near 22% before the report. They peaked around 41–49% during the day (Yahoo Finance, CNN), ended Wednesday around 35–37% (CNBC, Reuters), and were about 27% this morning (Reuters). The Fed meets Oct 27–28. The long end did not sell off by the close. The 10-year fell 2bp to 5.19% and the 30-year 4bp. CNBC reported that yields rose right after the report, then reversed lower as the stock drop sent some investors toward bonds; that is CNBC’s account, and the closes fit it. CNBC also reported yields falling further overnight. The 10-year has been at or above 5.19% since Sep 28. Before this run, it was last there in July 2007, and only briefly (Today in history, below).

On stocks, the data says “narrow,” not “broad.” It was the S&P 500’s first 1% drop since Jul 29 and its fifth loss in six sessions since the Oct 6 record (AP; this system’s closes agree). The Nasdaq’s 1.88% fall was its biggest since Jul 23, matching CNBC. But the selling clustered. The chip fund SMH fell 3.97%, and most of the biggest S&P decliners were AI-hardware, networking and power suppliers (Movers, below). The health-care fund rose 2.53% and consumer staples 2.22%; no named outlet this system found gave a reason for that move, so none is claimed. The average S&P stock (equal-weight RSP) fell 0.57%, about half the index. Small caps are the exception: the Russell 2000 fell 1.93% to its lowest close in six months, 11.04% under its Aug 14 high. Bloomberg called it a correction and tied it to rising rates; that link is Bloomberg’s. Two new claims test the next step: CL-0042 asks whether the AI repricing lasts, and CL-0043 whether credit treats Wednesday as a risk event.

Catching up on Monday and Tuesday (both editions failed to publish on a data gap). Monday was Columbus Day: bonds were closed and the S&P 500 ended near flat. CNBC’s wrap: “S&P 500 closes near flat, pressured by higher oil prices and memory chip stock losses.” NBC News reported energy prices rising after a Russia–Ukraine “energy ceasefire” announced by President Trump “fails to move Russia or Ukraine”; the Kremlin neither confirmed nor denied it. Tuesday the S&P 500 closed barely changed as JPMorgan, Citigroup, Wells Fargo and Goldman Sachs reported (CNBC: “S&P 500 closes near flat after big banks post earnings and memory chip stocks decline”). CNBC pointed to Broadcom CEO Hock Tan likening some AI investment to casino gambling, and to worries about Chinese memory-chip competition (CXMT). Also Tuesday, Reuters reported the IMF flagging “risks to global economy from AI market correction, war and debt” at its Bangkok meetings.

Oil is the link to inflation. WTI rose 1.01% Wednesday to $95.09, up 7.71% over five sessions and 65.6% this year. CNBC tied Wednesday’s rise to an IEA warning on market constraints and to Saudi officials saying Aramco facilities were attacked; Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said an administrative building at Aramco’s Dhahran headquarters was hit. Those reasons are CNBC’s, untested here. The mechanical link is in the CPI report itself: gasoline was more than half of September’s gain. Why this matters: higher gas prices hit household budgets directly, and they feed the inflation number the Fed is reacting to.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically (503 of 503 covered, plus all 50 megacaps); a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest), never by seeming interesting. 70 name candidates and 4 sector divergences qualified; cap is 3 names + 1 sector note, earnings and guidance reactions first. Left out: Skydance (SKYD, the former Paramount Skydance), the scan’s largest decline at −23.84%. Fox Business and Variety tied it to the company distributing nearly 471 million warrants to some shareholders. The NYSE lowered the prior close by about $0.19 to reflect the warrants, and the scan measures from the unadjusted $9.27, so about 2 points of the drop is that adjustment. A corporate action with no macro read-through. Everpure (P, −9.86%) had no company-specific reported reason.

Dell (DELL) −11.27% (507.93, from 572.47) — what happened: the biggest fall among AI-hardware names. HPE fell 8.28% and NetApp 7.03%; Ciena (−10.19%), Lumentum (−9.28%), Coherent (−9.19%), Marvell (−8.73%) and Super Micro (−8.42%) fell too. Stated reason: CNBC: “Dell stock plunges 11%, leading data center sell-off as fears mount about ‘enterprise AI timing.’” Barclays downgraded Dell, HPE and NetApp to equal weight (its neutral rating) from overweight, saying it doesn’t yet see a meaningful enterprise-AI inflection and that recent revenue strength reflects higher memory prices (CNBC, Yahoo Finance). Read-through: cycle-level. Barclays’ point is about when ordinary companies (enterprise buyers) start spending on AI hardware, as opposed to the giant cloud providers that have driven AI spending so far. That’s one broker’s view, not data. But it landed the same day as the financing worries in Tier 3, below.

Oracle (ORCL) −8.83% (130.55, from 143.20) — what happened: a reversal of Tuesday’s +4.23% (the close that refuted CL-0039, above). Stated reasons, three of them: Benzinga pointed to approval uncertainty for the gas pipeline serving Oracle’s Project Jupiter data center in New Mexico; Bloomberg reported Oracle asked federal regulators (FERC) for a fast ruling in an Oct 13 letter. The Motley Fool led with hotter CPI data lifting Treasury yields. CNBC framed it as contagion from CoreWeave’s bond selloff and AI-debt worries. This system adopts none of them as the cause. Read-through: Oracle is where the AI-financing story shows up in credit markets. Reuters reported this morning that its five-year credit default swaps (insurance against a default) widened 26bp overnight to a record 288bp, per S&P Global Market Intelligence; that record is S&P Global’s, not this system’s. Cycle-level; routed in Flags.

Bank of America (BAC) −4.76% (51.39, from 53.96) — what happened: a results-day drop, alongside Morgan Stanley (−2.75%) and State Street (−4.14%), which also reported. Stated reason: CNBC: “Bank of America shares drop after third-quarter revenue miss and regulatory penalty,” a $1.2 billion penalty over anti-money-laundering failures. Morgan Stanley beat estimates but fell; State Street topped the earnings view but missed slightly on revenue (Investing.com). Read-through: limited. The stated reasons are company-specific: a revenue miss and a regulatory charge. Nothing in the verified reporting points to loan losses or consumer credit, so no credit read-through is claimed.

Sector note — Health Care (XLV) +2.53% vs. SPY −1.08% (+3.62 points). Staples (XLP, +2.22%) and Energy (XLE, +0.64%) also beat the market; Technology (XLK, −2.98%) lagged by 1.90 points. Reuters’ midday report had health care and staples rising while the market fell, but no named outlet this system found gave a reason, so none is claimed. UnitedHealth (+4.73%), Moderna (+4.65%), Bristol-Myers (+4.61%), Merck (+3.80%) and Lilly (+3.62%) all cleared the scan. Read-through: the sectors least tied to the economic cycle rose while the most rate- and AI-sensitive one fell. That is the pattern a defensive rotation would leave, but here it is a hypothesis, not a finding; credit (CL-0043) is the independent check.
tier3_html: Daily read: SMH (this system’s chip-fund proxy for AI capex) fell 3.97% against SPY’s −1.08%. That’s its seventh straight daily decline, and it sits 15.57% below its Jun 22 six-month high. This week the financing side made the headlines. CNBC reported CoreWeave’s stock sank Wednesday as yields on its bonds neared 15% (a 14.8% yield to maturity on its 2032 notes). Reuters reported this morning that Oracle’s five-year credit default swaps widened to a record 288bp (S&P Global Market Intelligence), and that CDS on Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia also hit record wides, though far below Oracle’s. Earlier in the week, CNBC reported the Intel and Broadcom CEOs warning that capital and its cost could become the AI buildout’s biggest bottleneck. Semafor reported a data-center developer, Volta, marketing about $5 billion of debt at yields of at least 11% (final pricing unconfirmed). Bloomberg reported Blue Owl’s Stack Infrastructure seeking about US$6 billion for a Melbourne data center, a loan it first reported in July. Cycle-level reading: last week’s AI questions were about demand (OpenAI’s revenue figures, in the 10-09 and 10-10 editions). This week’s are about financing: what borrowed money costs the builders. The pressure showed up first in a weak borrower (CoreWeave) and a big borrower (Oracle), with the giant cloud providers’ CDS wider but far lower. That ordering is what the Lucent-pattern watch looks for, and it is a watch item, not a verdict. This system can’t see AI-specific credit directly: its HY OAS (3.16%, dated 10-13) is a broad junk-bond index. Why this matters: for a client heavy in AI-related stocks, the question this week is not only whether AI sells, but what it costs to build. CL-0042 tests whether the repricing lasts.
client_lens_html:
“Why did the market drop so much yesterday?” Two things landed on the same day: an inflation report a notch hotter than expected, and a sharp selloff in AI-related stocks. But it was narrower than the headline. The S&P 500 fell 1.11%, the average S&P stock about half that, and health-care and consumer-staples funds rose more than 2%. A diversified client likely felt less than the headline number. One honest caveat: small companies did fall hard, and the Russell 2000 is now more than 10% below its August high.

“Is the Fed going to raise rates again?” It’s more likely than it was on Tuesday, but still not the base case. The Fed raised rates in September and meets Oct 27–28. Market odds of an October hike, per CME FedWatch, went from about 22% before the CPI report to about 35–37% by Wednesday’s close (CNBC, Reuters), and were about 27% this morning (Reuters). For savers, that keeps CD and money-market yields high. For borrowers, mortgage rates are already 7.40% in the latest weekly survey.

“Should I be worried about my AI and tech stocks?” This week’s worry is less about whether AI is selling and more about the cost of building it. Barclays downgraded Dell and two other hardware makers on the timing of business AI spending (CNBC). The bonds and default insurance of some of the heaviest AI borrowers sold off (CNBC, Reuters). Whether that’s a lasting repricing or a one-week scare is open; this system’s test (CL-0042) grades it by Oct 21. For a client concentrated in this theme, it’s a reasonable moment to compare position size with the plan, not to react to one day.

Today, 8:30am ET, the follow-through on CPI. The producer price index (PPI, prices businesses get paid, a step before consumer prices): consensus +0.5% on the month in this system’s calendar, core +0.3%; the Dow Jones poll cited by CNBC has headline PPI at +0.6%. Retail sales: +0.3% (prior +1.2%). Weekly jobless claims: 195K (prior 197K). Philadelphia Fed manufacturing index: 26.5 (Investing.com’s calendar has 28.2; prior 37.8). Later: business inventories (10am), the Fed’s weekly balance-sheet release (H.4.1, this afternoon), the Fed’s Hammack (4:30pm), and Fed Chair Warsh at 11:30pm ET in a fireside chat with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at the IMF–World Bank meetings in Bangkok (IMF agenda, press reports). Friday: import prices, industrial production and capacity utilization, the federal budget, and foreign flows into U.S. securities (TIC).

Wednesday’s results: CPI +0.6% on the month (in line) and +3.7% on the year (3.6% expected); core +0.3% and +2.6% (0.2% and 2.5% expected), per CNBC citing the Dow Jones consensus. The Fed’s Beige Book (anecdotes from its 12 regional banks) said higher oil prices “permeated all District reports,” and five Districts noted firms reducing staffing or delaying hiring after investing in AI (Federal Reserve summary). Richmond Fed President Barkin said the CPI report “was higher than I would have hoped” and that the PPI data would help inform his inflation outlook (FXStreet).

Why this matters to the current regime: the Fed raised rates to 3.75–4.00% on Sept. 16 (CNBC) and meets again Oct 27–28. October hike odds went from near 22% before CPI to about 35–37% at Wednesday’s close, then about 27% this morning (CME FedWatch, per CNBC and Reuters); a hold is still the more likely outcome. Today’s data either add to the hike case or take some away. CL-0044 tests whether the 2-year moves with the surprise. Warsh speaks after this brief’s cutoff, so tomorrow’s edition covers it.
